title: "The housing-audit case"
subtitle: "Names and greetings in emails to public housing authorities, 2014"

---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tinytable)

audit <- read_csv("data/housing_audit.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
names_tab <- read_csv("data/display_names.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
outcomes <- read_csv("data/display_outcomes.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
analysts <- read_csv("data/analysts5.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
marks <- read_csv("data/reference_marks.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
curve <- read_csv("data/spec_curve.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
power <- read_csv("data/display_power.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
ri <- read_csv("data/display_ri.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Fixed decimals and a true minus sign, for every number on the page
fmt <- \(x, d = 1) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d) |> sub(pattern = "^-", replacement = "−")
pct <- \(x, d = 1) paste0(fmt(x, d), "%")
big <- \(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")
pe <- \(p) if (p < 0.001) "p < 0.001" else paste("p =", fmt(p, 3))

# one value from a display or record file, for inline use
grp <- \(g, col) names_tab[[col]][names_tab$level == "group" & names_tab$group == g]
mark <- \(id, col) marks[[col]][marks$id == id]
an <- \(id, col) analysts[[col]][analysts$id == id]
out <- \(o, cn, col) outcomes[[col]][outcomes$outcome == o & outcomes$contrast == cn]
pw <- \(design, gap) power$power[startsWith(power$design, design) & power$gap_pp == gap]
ref <- curve |> filter(is_reference)

counts <- audit |>
  mutate(no_thirds = if_any(c(white_third, black_third, hispanic_third, pop_third, poverty_third), is.na)) |>
  summarise(
    sent = n(),
    bounced = sum(is.na(reply)),
    delivered = sum(!is.na(reply)),
    replies = sum(reply %in% 1),
    uncoded = sum(reply %in% 1 & is.na(named)),
    coded = sum(reply %in% 1 & !is.na(named)),
    no_thirds_replies = sum(no_thirds & reply %in% 1),
    no_thirds = sum(no_thirds),
    no_assessment = sum(is.na(assessment_third))
  )

# P9W8Y, Task 1: in a model with the interaction of ethnicity and sex and the
# default treatment coding of R, the Type III test of ethnicity is the test
# among the female names, the reference level of sex
female <- audit |> filter(reply == 1, !is.na(named), name_sex == "female")
lr_female <- anova(glm(named ~ 1, family = binomial(), data = female),
                   glm(named ~ group, family = binomial(), data = female), test = "LRT")
p_female <- lr_female$`Pr(>Chi)`[2]

ri_band <- quantile(ri$b_pp, c(0.025, 0.975))
reply_range <- range(names_tab$reply_pct[names_tab$level == "group"])
gap_pooled <- grp("hispanic", "named_pct") -
  100 * (grp("white", "named") + grp("black", "named")) / (grp("white", "coded") + grp("black", "coded"))
oa_z <- abs(mark("OA", "statistic"))
oa_n <- mark("OA", "n")
oa_r <- tanh(oa_z / sqrt(oa_n - 3))

stat_txt <- \(type, x) case_when(
  is.na(x) ~ "none recorded",
  type == "chi2" ~ paste0("χ<sup>2</sup> = ", fmt(x, 3)),
  .default = paste(type, "=", fmt(x, 3))
)
```

This page presents the case on which the course is built, and every track starts here. The case is one claim from a field experiment on how officials of public housing authorities in the United States answer emails from people who want to apply for housing, published in the *American Journal of Political Science* by the original authors (OAs) [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect]. Five independent analysts reanalysed the claim in the Multi100 project, and a new experiment run for the SCORE programme tried to replicate it. The exercises begin where this page ends. Page numbers in quotations from the paper refer to the accepted manuscript, which is open at [OpenBU](https://hdl.handle.net/2144/37826).

## 1. The original study {#sec-study}

### 1.1 Street-level bureaucrats {#sec-question}

@Lipsky1980StreetLevelBureaucracy called the officials who deliver public services in direct contact with citizens 'street-level bureaucrats', a term that points to the discretion that they hold. The rules that they apply never settle every case, and how an official treats one applicant rather than another can decide who receives a benefit. Public housing in the United States is scarce and administered by local authorities under federal rules, and since 1998 those authorities have had wide freedom in selecting tenants, so that "local offices and officials have discretion over policies they did not themselves design" (p. 7). The OAs asked whether racial and ethnic bias, which earlier experiments had found among politicians and election officials, also reaches "bureaucracies that provide access to valuable government programs and are less tied to politics" (abstract). Their first hypothesis, from whose test the claim comes, reads "All else equal, bureaucrats will be less responsive and less friendly to blacks and Hispanics than they are to whites" (p. 5).

### 1.2 Audit studies {#sec-audits}

An audit study measures discrimination by sending requests that are identical except for one characteristic of the sender, assigned at random, and by comparing how they are answered. Sociology and economics made the design familiar through studies of hiring, with matched pairs of testers [@Pager2003MarkCriminalRecord] or with résumés that differed only in a name meant to indicate race [@BertrandMullainathan2004AreEmilyGreg], and a meta-analysis of such field experiments found no change since 1989 in hiring discrimination against African Americans, and some sign of a decline against Latinos [@QuillianEtAl2017MetaanalysisFieldExperiments]. Political science adapted the design to emails sent to state legislators [@ButlerBroockman2011PoliticiansRaciallyDiscriminate] and to local election officials [@WhiteEtAl2015WhatNeedVote], which found, as the OAs summarise them, that "blacks and Hispanics making queries about voting procedures are less likely to receive responses from state legislators and local election officials than whites" (p. 4). Because the characteristic is assigned at random, the groups of requests differ only by chance in everything else, and a difference in the answers can be read as its effect. What such a design manipulates, however, is a name, and a name tells its reader more than one thing about the sender, a point to which section 5 returns.

### 1.3 The design {#sec-design}

The OAs emailed "all public housing authorities that could plausibly be matched with a core city in a metropolitan or micropolitan area (n = 1017)", and "Each housing authority received an email on one of two days in the same week during 2014" (p. 8). Each authority was assigned at random to one of six email accounts, a male and a female name meant to indicate each of three groups (@tbl-names). The white and Black first names come from lists of names that are distinctive of each group, and the Hispanic names rely mainly on the surname Martinez, nearly 92% of whose bearers are Hispanic (p. 9). The OAs could match the ages that the white and the Black names suggest, but not those of the Hispanic names, which "peak in the 1990s and 2000s" (p. 10).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-names
#| tbl-cap: "The six names of the experiment, with the emails sent and delivered, the replies and the share of replies with a greeting code that opened with the name of the sender. Source: `data/display_names.csv`."
#| echo: false
names_tab |>
  filter(level == "name") |>
  mutate(group = factor(group, levels = c("white", "black", "hispanic"),
                        labels = c("White", "Black", "Hispanic"))) |>
  arrange(group, desc(name_sex)) |>
  transmute(
    Name = name,
    `Meant to indicate` = as.character(group),
    Sent = sent,
    Delivered = delivered,
    Replies = replies,
    `Reply rate` = pct(reply_pct),
    `Greeted by name` = pct(named_pct)
  ) |>
  tt() |>
  style_tt(j = 3:7, align = "r")
```

Every authority received the same text, with the name of the sender in place of X (p. 10).

> Hello,
>
> My name is X and I'm trying to figure out how to apply for public housing. I believe I may be eligible.
>
> Can you direct me to information about applying for public housing here? I also heard there might be a wait list for this program. How long is it?
>
> Thanks, X

For 45% of the authorities the address came from the list kept by the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), a case recorded as a 'Hard Email' (p. 11). The replies were coded for whether the authority replied at all, whether it replied within 24 hours, whether it gave the length of the wait list, and for tone, measured by "whether the emailer is addressed by proper name. We were lenient in coding 'yes.' A named salutation could be as causal [sic] as 'Hi Brett' or as formal as 'Dear Ms. Martinez.'" (p. 12). A cold reply can discourage an applicant, and the OAs argue that tone "can affect the ultimate distribution of benefits in subtle but important and under-appreciated ways" (p. 2).

### 1.4 The results {#sec-results}

The authorities replied at similar rates to every group, 60.7% to Black names against 57.5% to white names (p. 15). The gap of 4.8 points between white and Hispanic names is called "fairly small and borderline significant (with a one-tailed test)" (p. 15), with p = .11, and two-sided the same gap in the public file has `r pe(out("reply", "hispanic", "p"))`. Tone differed. "Sixty one percent of the messages to the white emailers began with a named salutation. Only 41% to Hispanics did." (p. 18). In the third model of Table 1, a logistic regression of the greeting on the three groups of names, with percent Black, percent Hispanic, poverty rate and logged population of the community (2012 American Community Survey) and the Hard Email indicator, the coefficient of the Hispanic names is −0.82 with a standard error of 0.22, on 549 replies (p. 37). As a change in the predicted probability of a named greeting from a white to a Hispanic name, with the other variables at their means, it is −20.0 percentage points, with a 95% confidence interval from −30.5 to −10.0 (p. 18). A footnote adds that coding every email without a reply as an unfriendly reply "does not affect the results" (p. 18, note 11), and officials with Hispanic names greeted Hispanic names by name not significantly more often than other officials did, 47% against 40% (p. 19).

```{r}
#| label: fig-names
#| fig-cap: "Share of replies with a greeting code that opened with the name of the sender, by name, with 95% Wilson intervals. Source: `data/display_names.csv`."
#| fig-alt: "Dot plot of six names with intervals. Brett, Emily and Tyrone lie near 60%, Shanice near 52%, Gabriela near 46% and Santiago near 37%; the two Hispanic names are drawn in burgundy."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3
#| echo: false
names_tab |>
  filter(level == "name") |>
  mutate(
    hispanic = group == "hispanic",
    name = reorder(name, named_pct)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = named_pct, y = name, colour = hispanic)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = named_lo, xmax = named_hi), size = 0.4, linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "#1d2731", `TRUE` = "#8b1538"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = \(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(20, 80)) +
  labs(x = "replies that open with the name of the sender", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

The abstract states the finding in the sentence from which the claim was taken: "Hispanic housing applicants were twenty percentage points less likely to be greeted by name than were their black and white counterparts" (abstract). The twenty points come from the comparison with white names. Against the white and Black names together, the raw gap among replies is `r fmt(gap_pooled)` points.

## 2. SCORE and Multi100 {#sec-score}

### 2.1 Reproduction, robustness and replication {#sec-repetition}

SCORE, short for Systematizing Confidence in Open Research and Evidence, put claims from published social and behavioural research through three kinds of repetition [@AlipourfardEtAl2021SystematizingConfidenceOpen]. A reproduction repeats the original analysis on the original data, a robustness check applies different but defensible analyses to the same data, and a replication asks the same question of new data. The three studies were reported in *Nature* in 2026 [@MiskeEtAl2026InvestigatingReproducibilitySocial; @AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness; @TynerEtAl2026InvestigatingReplicabilitySocial]. This paper went through two of them. Its data and code are public, but its reproduction component on the Open Science Framework (OSF) holds only an unfilled template, and the Multi100 record marks the reproduction as never attempted. The robustness study was Multi100, the subject of section 3, and section 5 takes up the replication.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The dossier on the OSF

- The SCORE project of the paper: [osf.io/3a8bg](https://osf.io/3a8bg/)
- Original materials: [osf.io/nrt4s](https://osf.io/nrt4s/)
- Reproduction with the data and code of the OAs, an unfilled template: [osf.io/9wp8d](https://osf.io/9wp8d/)
- Power analysis for the replication: [osf.io/kcsby](https://osf.io/kcsby/)
- Replication with new data, with its preregistration and final report: [osf.io/2ug8x](https://osf.io/2ug8x/)
- Multi100: [osf.io/38rsh](https://osf.io/38rsh/), with one component for each analyst – 8PTRZ [osf.io/j8wvh](https://osf.io/j8wvh/), UYV3F [osf.io/3672s](https://osf.io/3672s/) (a review document), EWFMI [osf.io/jhvca](https://osf.io/jhvca/), 25N5D [osf.io/v8zah](https://osf.io/v8zah/) and P9W8Y [osf.io/pzwbm](https://osf.io/pzwbm/)

The scripts of the analysts are read on the OSF, and the course does not copy them.
:::

### 2.2 The claim and the Task 2 instruction {#sec-multi100}

Multi100 gave claims from 100 studies in the SCORE sample to independent analysts, 457 people who carried out 504 reanalyses in all [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, p. 136]. Each claim is a sentence, taken from the abstract where possible, that corresponds to one statistically significant test, and where the lead team judged an expression "to be ambiguous or rhetorical, they replaced the expression with an ellipsis mark" [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, Methods]. This claim reached the analysts as follows.

> "Hispanic housing applicants were ... less likely to be greeted by name than were ... white counterparts" (p. 100 of the published article)

The ellipses remove "twenty percentage points" and "their black and". The claim as selected therefore compares Hispanic names with white names only and states a direction without a size, while the abstract compares them with Black and white names together and puts the gap at twenty points, and the five analysts tested both versions.

In Task 1 of Multi100 the analysts analysed the data as they judged best and drew one conclusion: evidence for the claim, evidence for the opposite, no evidence either way, or evidence for the null hypothesis. In Task 2 each produced a single statistical result under instructions that "always remained circumstantial (for example, data selection, exclusions and choice of measurement)" [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, Methods]. The instruction for this claim read as follows.

> "You should disregard the moving locations' ethnical composition from which/to which applications were sent."

Nobody in the experiment was moving, so the instruction can only mean that the ethnic composition of the communities, percent Black and percent Hispanic, should be left out of the model.

## 3. The five reanalyses {#sec-reanalysts}

All five analysts worked from the public file of the OAs. The course refits each analysis from its script, or for UYV3F from its report, on the same file, and the four recorded statistics come out exactly. @tbl-analysts sets out what each did in Task 2, under the identifiers that Multi100 gave them.

::: column-body-outset
```{r}
#| label: tbl-analysts
#| tbl-cap: "The five reanalyses in Task 2, with the statistic as Multi100 recorded it and the conclusion of Task 1. Source: `data/analysts5.csv`."
#| echo: false
analysts |>
  transmute(
    Analyst = id,
    Discipline = discipline,
    Hours = as.character(hours),
    Comparison = sub(" vs ", " against ", comparison),
    `Emails counted` = population,
    Method = method,
    `Emails analysed` = n_refit,
    `Recorded statistic` = stat_txt(statistic_type, statistic_recorded),
    `Task 1 conclusion` = task1
  ) |>
  tt() |>
  style_tt(j = c(3, 7), align = "r")
```
:::

### 3.1 Five questions {#sec-questions}

**UYV3F** compared Hispanic with white names among the replies, the comparison of the claim as selected, in a logistic regression without covariates. Such a model reproduces the two observed shares, so it estimates the raw gap of the paper, `r fmt(an("UYV3F", "b_pp_refit"))` points. The report states the hypotheses one-sided, "H0: β1 ≥ 0 vs. H1: β1 < 0".

**EWFMI** made the same comparison in Stata, in a model of all three groups, adjusted for the sex of the name, the Hard Email indicator and the poverty third of the community entered as a number from 1 to 3, after dropping the Hispanic third of the Task 1 model in line with the instruction. The adjusted gap is `r fmt(an("EWFMI", "b_pp_refit"))` points.

**8PTRZ** compared Hispanic names with the white and Black names together, the comparison of the abstract, with the test of a two-by-two table. `chisq.test()` in R applies a continuity correction to such a table by default, which makes the test slightly more conservative, and the recorded value is the corrected one. The gap is `r fmt(an("8PTRZ", "b_pp_refit"))` points, smaller than against white names alone because Black names were greeted by name less often than white ones.

**P9W8Y** fitted a logistic regression on all three groups and reported the test that the three differ at all, followed by pairwise comparisons. That omnibus test answers a broader question than the claim, since it would reject equality just as readily if the Black names were the ones greeted less often. The report gives a $\chi^2$ on 2 degrees of freedom, but Multi100 recorded no statistic, and the course places the analysis by its gap between Hispanic and white names, `r fmt(an("P9W8Y", "b_pp_refit"))` points.

**25N5D**, the one sociologist among the five, began from the comparison of the paper and then questioned it: "this naive estimate suffers from post-treatment bias. Signaled Hispanic names (the treatment) affect whether the bureaucrat responds; then, we condition only on bureaucrats who respond to investigate whether they use the applicant's proper name." Following @Coppock2019AvoidingPosttreatmentBias, the analyst counted every delivered email, an email without a reply counting as one without a named greeting. The gap shrinks to `r fmt(an("25N5D", "b_pp_refit"))` points and stays significant.

### 3.2 Comparing among replies {#sec-posttreatment}

The names were assigned to housing authorities at random, so the authorities that received each name are alike in expectation. The replies were not assigned at random. If the name changes whether an official replies, the officials who answered Santiago need not resemble those who answered Brett, and a comparison of greetings among replies mixes the effect of the name on how officials write with a difference in which officials wrote. Conditioning on a variable that the treatment can change is called post-treatment conditioning, and it can produce a difference between groups even where the treatment has no effect on the outcome [@MontgomeryEtAl2018HowConditioningPosttreatment]. @Coppock2019AvoidingPosttreatmentBias sets out the problem for audit experiments, in which the content of replies is a common outcome, and the redefinition that 25N5D chose is one of the remedies.

The remedy changes the question. Counting every delivered email keeps the groups as randomisation made them, so the gap of `r fmt(an("25N5D", "b_pp_refit"))` points is an effect of the name on receiving a reply that opens with the name of the sender. That outcome combines whether a reply came with how it began, and since only `r pct(reply_range[1], 0)` to `r pct(reply_range[2], 0)` of the emails in each group drew a reply, the gap among all emails is smaller almost by construction. The comparison among replies answers the question of the claim, about the tone of the replies that came, but it is a pure effect of the name only if the name did not change who replied. The gap in replies between white and Hispanic names, `r fmt(out("reply", "hispanic", "b_pp"))` points (`r pe(out("reply", "hispanic", "p"))`), makes a large selection unlikely without ruling it out. Both are defensible answers to two related questions, and the course keeps both.

### 3.3 Two verdicts of no evidence {#sec-verdicts}

Three analysts concluded in Task 1 that the data showed evidence for the claim. The other two ticked "The results do not show evidence for or against", although the work of each of them shows a significant gap. 25N5D concluded that "Hispanic housing applicants were less likely to be greeted by name than white applicants, though the magnitude of the effect is substantially smaller than that reported in the original results", so the verdict seems to judge the claim by the twenty points of the abstract, which the claim as selected had removed.

P9W8Y concluded that "The results do not provide evidence of a relationship between ethnicity and friendliness (proper name) on the received e-mails." The Task 1 model held the interaction of ethnicity with the sex of the name, and in such a model, with the default coding of R, the test of ethnicity compares the three groups among the female names alone, the reference category of sex. Refitted on the public file, the test of the three female names gives `r pe(p_female)`, the value that the analyst reported (0.13). In Task 2, without the interaction, the same analyst found that Hispanic names were greeted by name less often than white and Black names. One verdict rests on the size of the effect and the other on a narrower test than the analyst intended, and neither disputes the direction of the gap.

## 4. Effect sizes {#sec-scale}

The five results are a $\chi^2$ test of a table, a two-proportion test, two z statistics from logistic regressions and an omnibus test, on 362 to 665 emails. Multi100 chose to "transform the reported point estimates into a standard effect-size measure", noting that "these transformations have limitations and their calculation relies on assumptions that may not hold in all considered analysis settings" [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, p. 136]. Each statistic became a correlation and then a Cohen's d. For a z statistic the code of Multi100 uses the number of emails N in place of degrees of freedom, $r = \tanh(|z| / \sqrt{N - 3})$ with the sign of z, and a $\chi^2$ on one degree of freedom is read as the square of a z, which has no sign. @tbl-scale sets the correlations beside the gaps in percentage points.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-scale
#| tbl-cap: "The published result and the five reanalyses, with the gap in percentage points (the published change in predicted probability for the OAs, the course refit for the analysts) and the correlation by the Multi100 rule, signs as recorded. Sources: `data/reference_marks.csv`, `data/analysts5.csv`."
#| echo: false
bind_rows(
  tibble(Result = "OAs 2017", gap = mark("OA", "b_pp"), stat = paste("z =", fmt(oa_z, 2)),
         n = oa_n, r = oa_r),
  analysts |>
    transmute(Result = id, gap = b_pp_refit, stat = stat_txt(statistic_type, statistic_recorded),
              n = n_refit, r = r_recorded)
) |>
  transmute(
    Result,
    `Gap (points)` = fmt(gap),
    `Recorded statistic` = stat,
    `Emails in the conversion` = n,
    `r recorded` = if_else(is.na(r), "–", fmt(r, 3))
  ) |>
  tt() |>
  style_tt(j = c(2, 4, 5), align = "r")
```

The same gap gives different correlations. UYV3F and the OAs both report a gap of twenty points, yet their correlations are `r fmt(abs(an("UYV3F", "r_recorded")), 3)` and `r fmt(oa_r, 3)`, because one z comes from a model without covariates on `r an("UYV3F", "n_refit")` replies and the other from a model with covariates and all three groups on `r oa_n`. The `r fmt(abs(an("25N5D", "b_pp_refit")))`-point gap of 25N5D converts to almost as large a correlation as the `r fmt(abs(an("8PTRZ", "b_pp_refit")))`-point gap of 8PTRZ, because a correlation depends on the shares in each group and on the sizes of the groups as well as on the gap. The signs follow the statistics as the analysts typed them, so UYV3F carries a negative correlation, although all five found the gap in the direction of the claim. For the effect sizes Multi100 took the direction from the box that each analyst ticked, so that they "are negative only when they indicate an opposite effect compared with the original study" [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, Methods].

The course puts every result on the scale of the claim, the difference in the share of greetings in percentage points. A linear model of the 0/1 outcome gives it as its coefficient, and a logistic regression as an average marginal effect, the change in the predicted probability of a greeting from a white to a Hispanic name, averaged over the analysed emails. @fig-marks places the six results on that scale, beside the range of the `r nrow(curve)` specifications that the course fits.

```{r}
#| label: fig-marks
#| fig-cap: "The published result and the five reanalyses in percentage points, against the range of the specifications on the curve of the claim (shaded). Negative values mean that Hispanic names were greeted by name less often. Sources: `data/reference_marks.csv`, `data/spec_curve.csv`."
#| fig-alt: "Dot chart of six results between about −20 and −13 points, with a shaded band from −20.0 to −12.1 for the curve of the claim. 25N5D lies near −13, 8PTRZ near −17, the others near −20."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 2.8
#| echo: false
marks |>
  filter(on_chart, id != "SCORE") |>
  mutate(
    label = if_else(id == "OA", "OAs 2017", id),
    label = reorder(label, -b_pp),
    oa = id == "OA"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = b_pp, y = label, colour = oa)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = min(curve$b_pp), xmax = max(curve$b_pp), ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "#d6dde5", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "#9aa8b3") +
  geom_point(size = 2.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "#1d2731", `TRUE` = "#8b1538"), guide = "none") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-25, 2)) +
  labs(x = "gap in greetings by name, Hispanic minus comparison names (points)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

## 5. The replication {#sec-replication}

### 5.1 The design and the result {#sec-score-replication}

The SCORE replication ([osf.io/2ug8x](https://osf.io/2ug8x/)) was a preregistered experiment of the same kind. It emailed 3,050 public housing authorities listed by HUD, not only those matched to a core city, with block randomisation within each state, so that every state received equal numbers of Hispanic and white names. The names were new, Joe Garcia and Michael Hernandez against John Ryan and Nicholas Smith, chosen from pre-tested names that vary perceived ethnicity while keeping perceived class and migrant status similar. All four are male and none is meant to indicate a Black sender. The preregistration dropped the female names because, in its reading, the original study found no difference by the sex of the name, and the Black names because the claim does not concern them, which leaves more emails for each name. Replies were awaited for a week and coded as friendly if they used the first or the last name of the sender.

The authorities sent 1,811 replies. To match Table 1, the team kept the authorities in localities matched with census data, 2,337 emails and 1,243 replies, and fitted a logistic regression with the demographic covariates of the paper, from the 2018 American Community Survey and without the Hard Email indicator. On a random draw of 738 replies, the size set by the power analysis, the coefficient of the Hispanic names was 0.098 with a standard error of 0.149 (z = 0.66, p = 0.511), and on all 1,243 replies z = 0.44 (p = 0.657). Covariates in thirds gave the same picture. The preregistered linear probability model without covariates, on 1,000 random draws of 738 from the 1,484 replies of all authorities, found no significant difference "approximately 93 percent of the time". A logit coefficient of 0.098 corresponds to a gap of at most 2.45 points in favour of the Hispanic names. SCORE judged the claim not replicated.

### 5.2 Reading the replication {#sec-reading}

Within the original data the claim is hard to dislodge. Reshuffling the names at random among the replies to Hispanic and white names gives gaps between `r fmt(ri_band[1])` and `r fmt(ri_band[2])` points in 95% of `r big(nrow(ri))` reshuffles, far from the observed `r fmt(ref$b_pp)`, and all `r nrow(curve)` specifications of the curve of the claim are negative and significant, from `r fmt(min(curve$b_pp))` to `r fmt(max(curve$b_pp))` points. The replication shows that the same contrast, asked of a wider set of authorities in another year with other names, gave a gap close to zero, but it does not show which difference between the two studies is responsible.

The names are one candidate. Names that are meant to indicate the same group are not read in the same way: @Gaddis2017HowBlackAre found that names used in audits to indicate Black applicants vary in how often they are perceived as Black, and that names given more often by highly educated mothers are perceived as Black less often, so that the findings of an audit may depend on which names represent a group. The OAs could not match the ages of their Hispanic names, so Santiago and Gabriela may have suggested younger senders as well as a Hispanic background, while the replication chose its names to hold class and migrant status constant. Chance is another. The published interval runs from −30.5 to −10.0 points, and a study of this size detects a twenty-point gap almost always but a smaller one far less reliably. At a white rate of 61%, about 181 replies a group give a power of `r fmt(pw("original", 20), 2)` for a gap of 20 points, `r fmt(pw("original", 13), 2)` for 13 and `r fmt(pw("original", 10), 2)` for 10, against `r fmt(pw("replication", 10), 2)` for 10 points with the 369 a group of the replication. A significant estimate from a study with modest power for realistic effects tends to overstate their size. Time and place are a third candidate. The replication emailed the authorities on the HUD list, six years later, and a change in who answers such emails, or how, could move the result without either study being wrong.

The course is built around this contrast. On one set of data the claim survives every defensible analysis that the course can fit, and only its size moves. The analysts still disagreed on whether that was evidence for the claim, and new data found nothing, which is why the course treats robustness to analytic choices on one sample as a different property from replicability.

## 6. The data you will use {#sec-data}

The OAs published their data and code on the Harvard Dataverse ([doi:10.7910/DVN/1HOVTU](https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/1HOVTU)) under a CC0 licence, which places them in the public domain, so the course can redistribute the file and everything derived from it. The public file is blinded. Its ReadMe explains that census codes and continuous community values would identify the authorities, and that "Whether or not a housing official responded, particularly to an ostensible minority applicant, is very sensitive and potentially harmful information." Population, percent white, Black and Hispanic, the poverty rate and the HUD assessment score are therefore given only as thirds of their distributions (lower, middle and top). The experimental comparisons can be reproduced exactly, and the models with covariates only approximately: refitted on the thirds, the model of Table 1 gives z = `r fmt(mark("OA_blinded", "statistic"), 2)` and a gap of `r fmt(mark("OA_blinded", "b_pp"))` points, against the published z = `r fmt(mark("OA", "statistic"), 2)` and `r fmt(mark("OA", "b_pp"))` points. Nothing in the course tries to recover the continuous values.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-counts
#| tbl-cap: "The emails in the public file. Source: `data/housing_audit.csv`."
#| echo: false
tibble(
  Emails = c("In the public file (the paper reports 1,017)", "Bounced, with no reply status",
             "Delivered", "Replied", "Replied, without a greeting code", "Replied, with a greeting code",
             "Sent to authorities without community thirds", "Of these, replied",
             "Sent to authorities without a HUD assessment third"),
  Count = with(counts, c(sent, bounced, delivered, replies, uncoded, coded, no_thirds,
                         no_thirds_replies, no_assessment))
) |>
  mutate(Count = big(Count)) |>
  tt() |>
  style_tt(j = 2, align = "r")
```

The `r counts$bounced` bounced emails never reached an official, and the `r counts$uncoded` uncoded replies are replies whose greeting nobody coded. Both are decisions on the [specification menu](menu.qmd). `audit_original.csv` is the public file with the column names of the OAs, on which the reproduction of Task 3 runs ([codebook](data/audit_original_codebook.md)). `housing_audit.csv` is the course file, with readable names and derived columns, on which every other exercise runs ([codebook](data/housing_audit_codebook.md)). The [exercise overview](exercise.qmd) sets out what to do with them.
